topic.name: Calculating Flux in Two-Dimensional Vector Fields

question.text: Calculate the flux of the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y) = y\,\mathbf{i} - x\,\mathbf{j}$ across the closed curve $C$ given by $\mathbf r(t) = 5\cos t\,\mathbf{i} + 5\sin t\,\mathbf{j}$ for $t \in [0,2\pi).$
question.explanation:
If $\mathbf{F} = P\,\mathbf i + Q\,\mathbf j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is given by \[ \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = \oint\limits_{C}P\,\textrm d y - Q\,\textrm d x, \] where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$

Along the curve $C,$ we have \[ x = 5\cos t, \qquad y = 5\sin t. \]

Therefore,

\begin{align*} P(x,y) &= y = 5\sin t, \\[7pt] Q(x,y) &= - x = - 5\cos t. \end{align*}

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5\cos t) = -5\sin t, \\[10pt] \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5\sin t) = 5\cos t. \end{align*}

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

\begin{align*} \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s &= \oint\limits_C P \: \text{d}y - Q \: \text{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_0^{2\pi} \left(P \cdot \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} - Q \cdot \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \right) \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \int_0^{2\pi} \big( 5\sin t \big) \cdot \big( 5\cos t \big) - \big(- 5\cos t \big) \cdot \big( -5\sin t \big) \: \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] %&= \int_0^{2\pi} 25 \sin t \cos t - 25 \sin t \cos t \: \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \int_0^{2\pi} 0 \: \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= 0 \end{align*}

question.text: Calculate the flux of the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y) = y^2\,\mathbf{i} - xy\,\mathbf{j}$ across the closed curve $C$ given by $\mathbf r(t) = \cos t\,\mathbf{i} + 2\sin t\,\mathbf{j}$ for $t \in [0,2\pi).$
question.explanation:
If $\mathbf{F} = P\,\mathbf i + Q\,\mathbf j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is given by \[ \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = \oint\limits_{C}P\,\textrm d y - Q\,\textrm d x, \] where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$

Along the curve $C,$ we have \[ x = \cos t, \qquad y = 2\sin t. \]

Therefore,

\begin{align*} P(x,y) &= y^2 = 4\sin^2 t, \\[7pt] Q(x,y) &= -xy = -2\sin t \cos t. \end{align*}

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\cos t) = -\sin t, \\[10pt] \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\sin t) = 2\cos t. \end{align*}

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitution $\sin t = u, \cos t \,\mathrm d t = \mathrm d u,$ as follows:

\begin{align*} \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s &= \oint\limits_C P \: \text{d}y - Q \: \text{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_0^{2\pi} \left(P \cdot \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} - Q \cdot \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \right) \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \int_0^{2\pi} \big( 4\sin^2 t \big) \cdot \big( 2\cos t \big) - \big(-2\sin t \cos t \big) \cdot \big( -\sin t \big) \: \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \int_0^{2\pi} 8 \sin^2 t \cos t -2 \sin^2 t \cos t \: \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \int_0^{2\pi} 6 \cos t \sin^2 t \: \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \int_0^{0} 6 u^2 \: \textrm{d}u \\[5pt] &= 0 \end{align*}

example.title: Calculating the Flux of a Vector Field Over a Closed Curve in Parametric Form

question.text: Calculate the flux of the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y) = x\mathbf{i} + \dfrac{1}{4}\,\mathbf{j}$ across the closed curve $C$ given by $\mathbf r(t) = 4\cos t\,\mathbf{i} + 8\sin t\,\mathbf{j}$ for $t \in [0,2\pi).$
question.explanation:
If $\mathbf{F} = P\,\mathbf i + Q\,\mathbf j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is given by \[ \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = \oint\limits_{C}P\,\textrm d y - Q\,\textrm d x, \] where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$

Along the curve $C,$ we have \[ x = 4\cos t, \qquad y = 8\sin t. \]

Therefore,

\begin{align*} P(x,y) &= x = 4\cos t, \\[7pt] Q(x,y) &= \dfrac{1}{4}. \end{align*}

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\cos t) = -4\sin t, \\[10pt] \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(8\sin t) = 8\cos t. \end{align*}

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the double-angle formula for cosine, as follows:

\begin{align*} \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s &= \oint\limits_C P \: \text{d}y - Q \: \text{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_0^{2\pi} \left(P \cdot \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} - Q \cdot \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \right) \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \int_0^{2\pi} \left(4\cos t\right)\cdot \big( 8\cos t \big) - \left( \dfrac{1}{4}\right) \cdot \big( -4\sin t \big) \: \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \int_0^{2\pi} 32\cos^2 t + \sin t \: \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \int_0^{2\pi} 32\left(\dfrac{\cos(2t)+1}{2}\right) + \sin t \: \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \left(8\sin(2t) + 16t - \cos t\right) \Bigg|_0^{2\pi} \\[5pt] &= (0 + 32\pi - 1) - (0 - 1) \\[5pt] &= 32\pi \end{align*}

example.title: Calculating the Flux of a Vector Field Over a Closed Curve in Parametric Form

question.text: Calculate the flux of the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y) = y^3\,\mathbf{i} +(2+x)\,\mathbf{j}$ across the closed curve $C$ given by $\mathbf r(t) = 4 \cos t\,\mathbf{i} + 2 \sin t\,\mathbf{j}$ for $t \in [0,2\pi).$
question.explanation:
If $\mathbf{F} = P\,\mathbf i + Q\,\mathbf j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is given by \[ \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = \oint\limits_{C}P\,\textrm d y - Q\,\textrm d x, \] where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$

Along the curve $C,$ we have \[ x = 4\cos t, \qquad y = 2\sin t. \]

Therefore,

\begin{align*} P(x,y) &= y^3 = 8\sin^3 t, \\[7pt] Q(x,y) &= 2+x = 2 + 4\cos t. \end{align*}

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\cos t) = -4\sin t, \\[10pt] \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\sin t) = 2\cos t. \end{align*}

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitution $\sin t = u, \mathrm d u = \cos t\,\mathrm d t,$ as follows:

\begin{align*} \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s &= \oint\limits_C P \: \text{d}y - Q \: \text{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_0^{2\pi} \left(P \cdot \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} - Q \cdot \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \right) \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \int_0^{2\pi} \left(8\sin^3 t \right)\cdot \big( 2\cos t \big) - \left(2 + 4\cos t\right) \cdot \big( -4\sin t \big) \: \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \int_0^{2\pi} 16\sin^3 t \cos t +8\sin t + 16\sin t\cos t \: \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \int_0^{2\pi} 8\sin t \: \textrm{d}t + \int_0^{2\pi} 16\sin^3 t \cos t + 16\sin t\cos t \: \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \int_0^{2\pi} 8\sin t \: \textrm{d}t + \int_0^{0} 16u^3 + 16u \: \textrm{d}u \\[5pt] &= -8\cos t \Bigg|_0^{2\pi} +0 \\[5pt] &= 0 \end{align*}

example.title: Calculating the Flux of a Vector Field Over a Closed Curve in Parametric Form

question.text: Calculate the flux of the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y) =x^2\,\mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j}$ across the closed curve $C$ given by $\mathbf r(t) = 7\cos t\,\mathbf{i} + 2\sin t\,\mathbf{j}$ for $t \in [0,2\pi).$
question.explanation:
If $\mathbf{F} = P\,\mathbf i + Q\,\mathbf j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is given by \[ \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = \oint\limits_{C}P\,\textrm d y - Q\,\textrm d x, \] where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$

Along the curve $C,$ we have \[ x = 7\cos t, \qquad y = 2\sin t. \]

Therefore,

\begin{align*} P(x,y) &=x^2 =49 \cos^2 t, \\[7pt] Q(x,y) &= 1. \end{align*}

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(7\cos t) = -7\sin t, \\[10pt] \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\sin t) = 2\cos t. \end{align*}

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitution $\sin t = u, \mathrm d u = \cos t \,\mathrm d t,$ as follows:

\begin{align*} \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s &= \oint\limits_C P \: \text{d}y - Q \: \text{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_0^{2\pi} \left(P \cdot \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} - Q \cdot \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \right) \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \int_0^{2\pi} \left(49 \cos^2 t \right)\cdot \big( 2\cos t \big) - \left(1 \right) \cdot \big( -7\sin t \big) \: \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \int_0^{2\pi}98 \cos^3 t +7\sin t \: \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \int_0^{2\pi}98 \cos^2 t\cdot \cos t +7\sin t \: \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \int_0^{2\pi}98 (1-\sin^2 t) \cos t +7\sin t \: \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \int_0^{2\pi}98 (\cos t-\sin^2 t \cos t) +7\sin t \: \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \int_0^{2\pi}98 \cos t +7\sin t \: \textrm{d}t +\int_0^{2\pi} -98\sin^2 t \cos t\,\mathrm d t\\[5pt] &= \int_0^{2\pi}98 \cos t +7\sin t \: \textrm{d}t +\int_0^0 -98u^2\,\mathrm d u\\[5pt] &= \left( 98\sin t - 7\cos t\right) \Bigg|_0^{2\pi} +0 \\[5pt] &= 0 \end{align*}
